sourceObservations.observations: Lecture 23 title: Nonlinear and Time-Varying Systems; no separate technical assessment target.
Outline lists introduction, nonlinear/time-varying approach, nonlinear spring, nonlinear friction, inverted pendulum, its Python control, and MIMO systems.

The source contrasts independent constant-coefficient joint approximations with configuration-varying generalized inertia, motion-dependent coupling and nonuniform damping/dynamic effects. Configuration changes do not imply individual rigid link masses change.

The visible equation is tau=M(Theta) Theta_ddot+V(Theta,Theta_dot)+G(Theta). M is labelled symmetric positive definite and position-dependent; V vanishes at rest in the stated rigid velocity model; G is the torque needed against gravity. The bottom labels tau as unknown external torque and includes payload changes, so actuator torque, contact torque and model-parameter changes must be distinguished rather than silently merged.

Four separate sources of variation are payload, mechanical wear/friction/backlash/stiffness, motor heating/resistance, and external interaction. The absolute empty-hand controller fails with payload statement is too strong. Thermal torque effects depend on drive regulation and limits; fixed regulated current with fixed torque constant can maintain torque at increased voltage.

Three KUKA configurations show extended, folded and bent arm poses. They illustrate configuration effects but contain no numerical geometry, masses or axis data for a justified numerical inertia ranking.

The actual table contrasts local linearization near one operating point with moving linearization along a changing point. The moving model is linear but generally time-varying and remains approximate; the broad heading against linearization does not invalidate all local linear control.

The source claims fixed gains cannot retain poles but also says the standard servo part remains unchanged while model compensation handles nonlinearity. Under exact full-actuation/invertible-model cancellation, fixed normalized servo gains can indeed give fixed poles; physical compensation depends on state. Saturation, model mismatch and measurement error limit the claim.

The visible cubic curve runs through (-2,-8), (0,0) and (2,8), with odd symmetry and zero tangent at the origin. It is a signed constitutive term f=q x^3, not a nonnegative magnitude for all signed x. The tangent stiffness is 3q x^2, whereas q x^2 is secant stiffness; q carries N/m^3 units.

The positive x arrow and applied force point right; the cubic spring and damping arrows point left for positive x and xdot. The equation is m xddot+b xdot+q x^3=f. The desired physical closed-loop stiffness k_CL translates to normalized kp=k_CL/m and critical kv=2 sqrt(kp) after exact cancellation.

The partition shows alpha=m and beta=b xdot+q x^3 using actual state, followed by f_prime=xddot_d+kv edot+kp e. Both desired derivative dots in e and edot definitions are visible. f_prime is normalized acceleration, while beta is force.

The block diagram branches actual position/velocity into the cubic compensation. Desired-minus-actual comparators feed positive proportional/derivative corrections, then the mass scaling and positive model compensation. Algebra gives xddot=f_prime and homogeneous second-order error dynamics under exact matching, not a physically linear spring.

The explicit sign cases are +1, 0, -1 for positive, zero and negative velocity. The graph instead has filled dots at both +bc and -bc on the zero-speed axis, inconsistent with the single-valued printed definition. Use the declared code sign convention and separately qualify static friction. The resistance term is on the equation left; the physical friction force opposes velocity.

This example changes from a cubic spring and viscous friction to a linear spring and Coulomb friction: m xddot+bc sgn(xdot)+kx=f. The free-body arrows are left for the spring and positive-velocity resistance, right for positive applied input; do not silently carry the prior cubic/viscous terms over.

The model compensation is alpha=m, beta=bc sgn(xdot)+kx, with actual position and velocity. The servo retains desired acceleration plus positive desired-minus-actual error terms. The displayed expanded input line appears to omit its equals sign, but the partition and subsequent page make the intended equality explicit.

The full plant and controller equations visibly match Coulomb and spring terms, leaving m xddot=m f_prime and xddot=f_prime. This cancellation uses the same sign convention and exact parameters; an estimated Coulomb coefficient would leave a signed residual.

The source derives eddot+kv edot+kp e=0 and states gain-dependent damping and possible critical damping. The top substitution line appears to have only one desired-x dot although the preceding servo law and the twice-differentiated error require desired acceleration. The final error relation is consistent with the acceleration-feedforward interpretation, not a velocity term added to acceleration.

The single-joint link diagram measures theta counterclockwise from the rightward horizontal and gravity downward. The motor torque arrow is counterclockwise. A massless rigid link with a point mass at fixed distance l has constant I=m l^2 despite nonlinear gravity and Coulomb friction. Geometry dependence does not mean angle-dependent inertia in this particular one-link model.

The actual slide writes tau = ml^2 theta_ddot + v theta_dot + c sgn(theta_dot) + mgl cos(theta). Alpha is ml^2 and beta uses actual angle and speed. The diagram measures theta counterclockwise from the rightward horizontal; physical gravitational torque is -mgl cos(theta), explaining the positive left-side term.

The normalized servo law is desired angular acceleration plus kv times velocity error plus kp times position error, with desired-minus-actual errors. Substitution into the matched plant cancels actual-state gravity and friction, leaving theta_ddot = f_prime.

The top substitution appears to print a single dot on desired theta, whereas the block diagram feedforward has two dots and the subsequent error equation requires desired acceleration. Preserve this apparent typographical error rather than treating desired velocity as acceleration. The normalized command precedes multiplication by ml^2 and addition of actual-state compensation.

The actual Python image defines a constant 90-degree desired angle converted to radians and zero desired angular velocity and acceleration. Parameters are m=l=1, I=m*l**2, viscous coefficient 0.6, Coulomb coefficient 0.4, g=9.81, kp=16 and kv=8. Imports are not visible.

The control_torque image unpacks actual theta and speed; computes desired-minus-actual position and velocity errors; forms normalized desired acceleration plus the two feedback terms; and returns torque, error, velocity error and normalized command. Torque includes actual-state viscous friction, np.sign Coulomb friction and cosine gravity.

The plant_dynamics image obtains the first controller return value, subtracts actual viscous, Coulomb and gravity terms, divides by I and returns [theta_dot, theta_ddot]. solve_ivp is called with [t0,tf], x0, t_eval and rtol=atol=1e-8, but imports and initialization are not printed on this slide. Any reconstructed horizon, sample count or initial condition must be explicitly supplied rather than attributed to this code.

The plotted position starts near -20 degrees and approaches the dashed 90-degree target over a displayed 0–8 s range. The lower-left axes show error and error derivative, not a separately labelled actual-velocity trace; error derivative reaches about -2.8, so actual velocity is positive for a constant target. Torque starts near 40 N m and approaches a small positive value on the shown scale. These nominal plots do not establish robustness or exact finite-time zero error.

The animation still explicitly displays Time=0.00 s, Error=1.9199 rad and Torque=39.94 N.m. Actual unit link points right and downward near (0.94,-0.34), desired dashed link is vertical. Phase portrait axes are theta in radians and theta_dot in rad/s, beginning near (-0.35,0) and tracing a positive-speed arc toward (pi/2,0). A screenshot is not evidence of executing animation in the study app.

The slide changes from SISO to multiple coupled equations, vector inputs and outputs, desired joint positions/velocities/accelerations, and vector actuator torques or forces. Multiple joints alone does not imply the inertia matrix is diagonal.

The printed partitioned vector law is F=alpha F_prime+beta. F, F_prime and beta are n-by-1; alpha is n-by-n and explicitly not necessarily diagonal. Exact linearization/decoupling is conditional on correct alpha and beta. Independent unit-mass behavior is a normalized mathematical model, not a change of physical link mass.

The vector servo law contains desired acceleration, Kv times velocity error and Kp times position error; E=Xd-X. Both gain matrices are n-by-n and displayed diagonally with independently indexed gains. Diagonal servo gains after compensation do not imply an originally diagonal manipulator inertia matrix.

This summary repeats constant-coefficient limitations, nonlinear/time-varying and partitioned control, nonlinear spring and Coulomb models, pendulum simulation, and MIMO extension. No new equation or independent numerical premise appears.
References only: KUKA Robotics and Craig, Introduction to Robotics: Mechanics and Control, third edition, 2004. No new examinable technical content.
Thank You closing slide only; no substantive examinable content.

independentAnswers.reasoning: The same fixed link masses have configuration-dependent moment arms, so generalized inertia can vary without any mass change.
In the stated rigid-body decomposition, V collects velocity-product Coriolis and centrifugal/centripetal terms; G is gravity and M multiplies acceleration.
Positive kinetic energy in independent nonsingular generalized coordinates gives a symmetric positive-definite mass matrix, generally dependent on configuration.
With positive contact torque defined as assisting the positive coordinate, generalized input is the sum tau_a + tau_ext on the right side.
A payload changes distributed inertia and gravitational loading, and can alter the velocity-product terms through changed dynamic parameters; it is not just a fixed scalar disturbance.
An empty-hand controller can lose tracking quality or margin with a payload; universal inevitable failure is not justified without plant, gains and limits.
With fixed torque constant and ideal current regulation within voltage limits, the same current gives the same torque, while increased resistance requires greater voltage.
The photographs demonstrate qualitatively different configurations; they do not supply quantitative inertial parameters or a reliable exact ranking.
A linearization evaluated along a changing trajectory generally has time-varying coefficients.
Check local approximation validity and operating-region variation rather than declaring every linear model invalid everywhere.
Exact state-dependent compensation can leave fixed normalized servo gains and fixed nominal error poles; physical compensation still changes with state.
When the actuator saturates, applied input differs from requested cancellation input, so the ideal homogeneous error equation need not hold.
For the signed constitutive term q x^3, q has units N/m^3 and the tangent derivative is 3q x^2. The stem calls this a magnitude without restricting x>=0, which needs qualification.
Replacing x by 2x scales q x^3 by eight and its tangent 3q x^2 by four.
The visible (-2,-8) and (2,8) points reflect an odd cubic law, not an even force magnitude.
For positive displacement and velocity, spring and viscous damping exert restoring/opposing forces -q x^3 and -b x_dot; the applied force is positive rightward.
Normalize physical stiffness by mass: kp=18/2=9 s^-2; critical kv=2 sqrt(9)=6 s^-1.
The normalized command is acceleration, with translational units m/s^2, before multiplication by mass and addition of force compensation.
Substituting f=m f_prime+b x_dot+q x^3 into the identical plant leaves m x_ddot=m f_prime and hence x_ddot=f_prime.
E=xd-x and exact x_ddot=xd_ddot+kv E_dot+kp E give E_ddot+kv E_dot+kp E=0.
Compensation must use actual displacement and speed to cancel the actual plant terms, not desired-state substitutions.
Viscous resistance magnitude scales with |velocity|, whereas ideal Coulomb resistance has constant nonzero-speed magnitude.
Use the explicitly declared sign(0)=0 convention; the zero-speed graph endpoints and actual stiction need qualification rather than silently equating them.
At negative velocity, physical Coulomb friction is -0.4 sign(-2)=+0.4 N, opposing the motion.
The new model is m x_ddot+bc sign(x_dot)+k x=f, with a linear spring and Coulomb friction, not the previous cubic spring/viscous model.
Beta is bc sign(actual velocity)+k actual position, with the same signs as the left-side plant terms.
The mismatched plant gives x_ddot=f_prime+(bhat-b)sign(v)/m. Therefore the error equation has forcing (b-bhat)sign(v)/m.
s^2+8s+16=(s+4)^2 has a stable repeated negative root and is critically damped.
For counterclockwise angle from the rightward horizontal, gravity produces physical torque -mgl cos(theta), so the left-side term is +mgl cos(theta).
The fixed point mass on a massless rigid link has constant I=ml^2; gravity cosine and Coulomb sign terms make the second-order dynamics nonlinear.
At rest with sign(0)=0, holding torque is mgl cos(theta): 9.81 N m at zero angle and zero at pi/2 for unit m and l.
Beta uses actual speed in viscous/Coulomb terms and actual angle in gravity, matching the plant nonlinearities.
Desired angular acceleration is required by both dimensions and differentiating the desired-minus-actual error twice; a single desired derivative dot is a source typo.
The normalized angular acceleration command must be multiplied by ml^2 before adding torque compensation.
The reference is the constant pi/2 rad angle; its first and second time derivatives are both zero.
I=m l^2 has units kg m^2; v and c are distinct viscous and Coulomb coefficients; kp and kv are normalized servo gains with s^-2 and s^-1 units.
The function returns the actuator torque followed by position error, velocity error and normalized acceleration command.
E=pi/2-pi/6=pi/3 rad and E_dot=0-0.5=-0.5 rad/s.
NumPy trigonometric functions require radians, so 90 degrees must become pi/2 before use in the controller/model.
The two-state derivative is [theta_dot,theta_ddot], corresponding to state [theta,theta_dot].
Underscores receive the three discarded diagnostics when unpacking a four-value return; they neither zero the diagnostics nor change the function result.
The solver tolerances request numerical integration accuracy; they neither prove physical-model accuracy nor impose exact zero tracking error.
Imports plus t0, tf, x0 and t_eval must be supplied for a standalone execution; their values are not printed by the shown solve_ivp call.
Initial desired-minus-actual error is (90-(-20))*pi/180=11*pi/18, approximately 1.919862177 rad.
Initial speed and sign are zero. Torque is 16*(11*pi/18)+9.81*cos(-pi/9)=39.93617945 N m, approximately 39.94, including positive gravity compensation.
For the repeated root -4, E=(A+Bt)e^-4t. E(0)=E0 gives A=E0 and E_dot(0)=0 gives B=4E0, so E=E0(1+4t)e^-4t.
Actual speed is -E_dot=16E0 t e^-4t. Differentiating gives 16E0 e^-4t(1-4t), so the peak occurs at t=0.25 s.
The depicted nominal matched-model response is evidence for that example, not proof of robustness to uncertain payload, saturation or sensor defects.

For every finite positive time on the exact trajectory, actual speed is positive so Coulomb compensation remains +c. Its limiting torque can approach c although the controller value at the exact zero-speed equilibrium uses sign(0)=0 and is zero.
The unit link endpoint is (cos(-20 degrees),sin(-20 degrees)), approximately (0.93969,-0.34202) m.
The phase portrait axes are actual angle in radians and angular velocity in radians per second, not time versus angle.
The still supports its displayed instantaneous geometry and labels, not a claim that animation code has been executed inside this offline app.
Differentiate the specified quadratic desired trajectory componentwise: position t^2 gives velocity 2t and acceleration 2 with the stated dimensional coefficient.
An off-diagonal M_ij multiplies acceleration of coordinate j in generalized force equation i, representing inertial coupling.
For n generalized coordinates, alpha is n-by-n and F, F_prime and beta are n-by-1 vectors.
A full, correctly matched invertible mass matrix can cancel inertial coupling; requiring alpha itself to be diagonal would generally prevent that cancellation.
Matrix multiplication gives [2*1+1*(-2),1*1+3*(-2)]=[0,-5]; adding [0.5,1] yields [0.5,-4].
Diagonal normalized gain matrices independently shape each decoupled error coordinate, without claiming the physical mass matrix is diagonal or masses equal one.
Componentwise critical damping requires Kv=diag(2*sqrt(9),2*sqrt(25))=diag(6,10).
With exact vector cancellation, E=Xd-X gives E_ddot+Kv E_dot+Kp E=0 componentwise for the displayed diagonal gains.
